title: Before moving
hookLine: an unsend button gives a few seconds' grace; Shantideva moves the check earlier, even before a glance
tomorrow: the body: something to worship, or a boat to cross in?

cards: Some email apps have an unsend button: a few seconds of grace after you hit send, in case you wake up. People love it. It saves friendships.
But by the time you're reaching for unsend, the message has already left your hands. Here's an odd thing about chapter five. Shantideva gives instructions about where to put your eyes.
When to look down, when to look around, when to look up. Why would a guide to compassion bother with a glance?

teach.h: GAZE DOWN, LOOK UP, GREET THEM.
teach.b: First, the strange detail. He tells the practitioner to keep the gaze lowered and steady, and to look around now and then to rest the eyes. And if someone comes into view, look up and greet them.
It sounds fussy, like a rulebook for posture. Then the key verse arrives.
When you wish to move, or wish to speak, first examine your own mind, then act, steadily. That's the answer to the puzzle. A glance is the smallest movement there is.
If you can catch the mind before a glance, you can catch it before a step, a word, a sent message.
The glance is practice for the big moments, the way scales are practice for a song.
The guard from day one of the chapter, mindfulness, has a partner here: alertness, samprajanya, the part of you that checks what's happening right now. Yesterday's log is the brake.
Today is noticing the hill before the car starts rolling.
Before moving, before speaking, even before looking: one quick look inward. What's the mind doing? Then go.

how: In monastic training and in lay practice, Buddhists cultivate alertness (samprajanya, Pali sampajanna) by paying attention to ordinary movements, walking, looking, reaching, speaking, as they happen.

o: asking a teacher's permission before doing anything
stretching your body before a long walk or a run
checking your mind before you move, speak or look

games.q: the puzzle of the glance — tap the pairs.
p: lowered and steady, resting now and then

s: Shantideva's eye instructions are just old-fashioned manners
they train the mind to check itself before the smallest movement.
he says to look up and greet someone who comes into view
the lowered gaze isn't a wall; people still get a greeting.

games.q: your roommate's dishes have sat in the sink for three days. you're getting up to go knock on her door. by Shantideva's verse, when do you check your mind?
o: once she opens the door and you can see what mood she's in.
right now, before the first step: what is my mind doing?
afterward, so you can learn what went wrong in the talk.
games.why: first examine your own mind, then act. the check comes before the first step, not after the door opens.

practice: Rest one hand near something you can pick up, a cup, a pen, your phone. Before the hand moves, pause and check: what's my mind doing right now?
Then lift it slowly, set it down, and do it once more, catching the moment just before the move.

wordCard.voice: Before moving: Shantideva's earliest check. Look at your own mind first, then move, speak or look, steadily.

orig.note: Sanskrit: alertness, clear knowing of what you're doing as you do it. Pali sampajanna.

carryVoice: Keep this line close: check first, a glance inward before the glance outward. Chapter five rolls on.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 5.35-5.37 (keep the gaze lowered; look around now and then to rest the eyes; if someone appears, look and greet them) and 5.47 (when wishing to move or speak, first examine one's mind, then act with steadiness)
